problem: The trap contradicts the chapter's own (correct) density rule. A density of 2×10⁻³ V/Hz multiplied by a 1 Hz filter width gives exactly 2×10⁻³ V = 2 mV, so the sentence 'A value of 2×10−3 V/Hz is not 2 mV at the output of a 1 Hz filter' is false. A student who follows the instruction 'multiply by the filter width' gets 2 mV and then reads that this is wrong.
fix: Rewrite: 'X(f) is a density in V/Hz. Multiply it by the filter width in hertz to get volts. Around f = 0 the pulse has 2 mV/Hz, so a flat 1 Hz filter passes a peak of 2 mV; a filter many times wider passes proportionally more, because the density is being added over a wider band.'

problem: 'A system is distortionless when every frequency gets the same gain and a delay that grows linearly with frequency' is wrong as written: in a distortionless system the time delay is the same for every frequency. What grows linearly with frequency is the phase lag in radians, θ(f) = −2πf t_d. The sentence teaches the opposite of the formula given two lines later.
fix: 'A system is distortionless when every frequency gets the same gain and the same time delay. In phase terms θ(f) must be a straight line through the origin, θ(f) = −2πf t_d: the phase lag in radians grows linearly with frequency, while the delay t_d stays constant.'

problem: The 3-dB bandwidth is quoted as 0.443/T. That number is only the offset of one half-power point from f = 0; the full 3-dB bandwidth, the width between the two half-power points, is 2 × 0.443/T = 0.886/T. Since the whole chapter insists on naming the bandwidth definition, giving the half-width as 'the 3-dB bandwidth' is a wrong number students will memorise.
fix: '|X(f)| falls to 1/√2 of its peak at f = ±0.443/T, so the 3-dB bandwidth, peak to peak between these two points, is 0.886/T ≈ 0.89/T. That is a different number from the null-to-null 2/T.'

problem: 'Sampling x_I and x_Q needs only B samples per second' is ambiguous. Each component has bandwidth B/2, so each needs B samples per second; the two together need 2B real samples per second. As written it suggests the total is B.
fix: 'x_I needs B samples per second and x_Q needs B samples per second, so the pair needs 2B real samples per second, far below the 2f_c samples per second the 100 MHz carrier itself would demand.'

problem: The property line shifts the spectrum by one complex exponential, but the next sentence says a carrier moves it to ±f_c. Multiplication by e^(j2πf_c t) moves the spectrum to +f_c only; the two-sided shift comes from multiplying by cos(2πf_c t). A student can carry away the wrong rule.
fix: 'x(t) e^(j2πf_c t) ↔ X(f − f_c): a complex exponential shifts the spectrum one way, to +f_c. Multiplying by a real carrier cos(2πf_c t) = ½(e^(j2πf_c t) + e^(−j2πf_c t)) makes two half-size copies at ±f_c; that is modulation.'

problem: The plotted copy at 10 kHz peaks at 1 mV/Hz, half the 2 mV/Hz of the baseband sinc, yet the caption says the shifted copy 'keeps the same shape and width' and the aria text calls it an 'identical sinc'. The halved height is the correct result of modulation by a unit-amplitude cosine, but the caption never says so and the aria text contradicts the data.
fix: Add to the caption: 'The shifted copy has the same sinc shape and width but half the height, 1 mV/Hz, because a unit-amplitude cosine splits the amplitude between +f_c and −f_c; only the +f_c copy lies inside this plot.' Change 'identical sinc' in the aria text to 'half-height sinc'.

problem: Exponents and powers are typed as plain characters in the running text, so 'ej2πft', 'e−j2πf t₀', 'ejθ(f)', 'sinc(103 f)' and '2×10−3' read as multiplications (e times j2πft, 10 to the 3 times f). Several formulas in the same chapter do use <sup>, so the page looks inconsistent.
fix: Use <sup> or Unicode superscripts everywhere: e^(j2πft) as e<sup>j2πft</sup>, 10⁻³, 10³ f, θ(f) exponents, and in step 4 and the answer line write X(f) = 2×10⁻³ sinc(10³ f) V/Hz.
